typical_award_size: FY 2026-27 NOFA: $8,000,000 available (up from $1,500,000 in FY 2025-26 and $1.5M in FY 2024-25). FY 2025-26 awards: Freebird Development, Healdsburg, 42 units, $1,340,417; Burbank Housing, Guerneville, 21 units, $159,583. Minimum loan $100,000; maximum limited to one program year's funds unless the Board commits future years. Since 2003 the fund has invested over $24M in more than 550 homes.
affordability_requirement: Rental: all assisted units affordable 55 years, initially to very low income (50% AMI), may float up to low income (80% AMI) on turnover. Priorities: most units at lowest incomes, geographic distribution across cities and unincorporated area, Housing Opportunity Sites, integration with health and human services, PSH and special needs. Homeownership: first-time buyers at or below 120% AMI with 20% of units at 80% AMI.
layering_notes: Sonoma's main local gap source, capitalized by County General Fund, Reinvestment and Revitalization Funds (former RDA), developer in-lieu fees from the residential Affordable Housing Program, non-residential Workforce Housing fees, countywide transient occupancy tax, and loan repayments. Residual receipts loans structured to be compatible with LIHTC investor requirements; interest set by the Commission. Awarded in one annual NOFA together with HOME, CDBG, ESG and LMIHAF so applicants file once. Funds may go to projects inside cities only where the city has a RHNA Sharing Agreement with the County (shelters and congregate facilities exempt). Sponsors must comply with the County Living Wage Ordinance; the policy is silent on prevailing wage, so the Labor Code 1720(c)(6)(E) below-market-loan exemption may apply unless HOME or CDBG is also used. The County does not act as a conduit bond issuer; recent Sonoma deals used CMFA (Burbank Housing $8.12M) and CalHFA. CFH awards are typically $1M to $3M and are counted as local leverage for CTCAC tiebreaker and CDLAC readiness.

program_name: RED Housing Fund (Renewal Enterprise District, PG&E wildfire settlement capital)
administering_agency: RED Housing Fund, a nonprofit capitalized with $10M each from the County of Sonoma and the City of Santa Rosa (PG&E 2017 fire settlement), affiliated with the Renewal Enterprise District JPA
typical_award_size: Round 2 (NOFA issued March 4, 2026, due April 1, 2026): up to $5,000,000 in loans. Loan size up to 10% of project cost. Affordable projects: subordinate or senior loan at 3% interest, interest only during construction and up to 36 months after conversion, then amortizing, up to 18-year combined term, sized at minimum 1.05 combined DSC. Market rate or middle income: construction loan at senior rate plus 1% (4% floor), up to 3 years; permanent loan at first-position rate plus 1% (4% floor), up to 10 years. 1% origination fee ($10,000 minimum); commitments expire 18 months after Board approval. Round 1 (December 21, 2021 NOFA) awards: Acme Family Apartments $800,000, Aviara $2,400,000, Casa Roseland $4,200,000, 420 Mendocino Avenue $7,000,000, Pullman Lofts $2,300,000 (reduced to $1,300,000), South Park Commons $4,000,000.
affordability_requirement: Infill, mid- to high-density residential or mixed-use projects in transit-rich or planned areas meeting RED criteria; income mix may be affordable (up to 80% AMI), middle income (80% to 120% AMI), market rate, or mixed.
layering_notes: Lender of last resort (recycling repaid settlement capital) for projects the County and Santa Rosa want built in downtown Santa Rosa and other priority development areas; it accepts market-rate and middle-income deals that cannot use CFH or LIHTC. Capital is public settlement money, so prevailing wage exposure depends on loan terms. The separate private Sonoma County Housing Fund ($10M, Housing Trust Silicon Valley with the Santa Rosa Metro Chamber, predevelopment and acquisition loans up to five years) belongs in Pass 4.

program_name: Tax-exempt multifamily bonds: no County or YCH conduit program; CMFA and CSCDA issuances with local TEFRA approval
administering_agency: Issuers California Municipal Finance Authority and California Statewide Communities Development Authority; TEFRA approval by the host city council or, in the unincorporated area, the Yolo County Board of Supervisors
typical_award_size: Project-sized conduit issuances. Example: CMFA issued $6,668,698 of tax-exempt bonds for Esperanza Crossing Apartments (Mercy Housing, 40 units on Woodland Avenue, 39 units at or below 55% AMI). No County of Yolo or Yolo County Housing bond issuance and no County TEFRA resolution appeared in the 2026 Board minutes reviewed (January 27, March 3 and March 24, 2026).
affordability_requirement: Federal bond and 4% LIHTC rules: at least 20% of units at 50% AMI or 40% at 60% AMI (or income averaging), 55-year CDLAC regulatory agreement.
layering_notes: Neither the County nor YCH runs a bond program, so budget issuer fees for CMFA or CSCDA. Bonds alone do not trigger state prevailing wage, but tax credits plus state or County funds in the same deal usually do. The County's TEFRA practice in the unincorporated area could not be confirmed from opened documents because no recent unincorporated bond-financed project was found.

program_name: Behavioral Health Services Act Integrated Plan FY 2026-29 (Housing Interventions component)
administering_agency: San Benito County Behavioral Health Department (Rachel White, Director)
typical_award_size: Integrated Plan FY 2026-29 approved by the Board June 23, 2026 (4-0) after DHCS approval May 28, 2026 and a public hearing May 21, 2026. Statutory split is 30% Housing Interventions, 35% Full Service Partnerships and 35% Behavioral Health Services and Supports, but the County transferred 7% each from FSP and Housing Interventions into BHSS (about 23% Housing Interventions). The State approved spending up to 35% of the Housing Interventions component on capital development (above the standard 25%) for a housing development project with the Health and Human Services Agency to house HHSA and Behavioral Health clients experiencing homelessness. Dollar amounts are in the plan and budget attachments, not the staff report.
affordability_requirement: BHSA eligible adults and youth with serious mental illness or substance use disorder; at least 50% of housing funds for chronically homeless people under state law unless exempted.
layering_notes: San Benito County is a small non-entitlement county with no housing department: the Resource Management Agency (Planning and Building, Abraham Prado, (831) 637-5313) administers the inclusionary ordinance, in-lieu fees, density bonus and TEFRA hearings; the Health and Human Services Agency (Community Services and Workforce Development) runs HHAP, the shelter and the Migrant Center; Behavioral Health holds BHSA; and the Housing Authority of the County of Santa Cruz administers vouchers and PBVs for Hollister and San Juan Bautista. The County has no HOME or CDBG entitlement, no housing trust fund NOFA and no County loan program; Hollister runs its own PLHA and CDBG programs (Pass 3). sanbenitocountyca.gov and the amlegal code library block automated access, so records were built from Board of Supervisors packets on cosb.granicus.com (attachments on d2kbkoa27fdvtw.cloudfront.net), HCD allocation tables and hacosantacruz.org. Classified as grant because the approved plan funds housing capital (a County-HHSA development project using up to 35% of Housing Interventions) and interim and permanent housing for clients. For a county of about 68,000 people the Housing Interventions share is small after the 7% transfer to BHSS; a developer's realistic entry is partnering on the County-HHSA project or an operating subsidy on a few PSH units. Source is the June 23, 2026 Board packet; the plan and budget attachments are on cloudfront via the June 23 agenda.

program_name: County affordable housing grant for Eastern Madera County (up to $1,643,522, approved September 14, 2021)
administering_agency: Madera County Board of Supervisors and Community and Economic Development Department
typical_award_size: On September 14, 2021 (item 6.b, file 7750) the Board unanimously approved up to $1,643,522 over five years for predevelopment, development, acquisition, rehabilitation or preservation of multifamily, live-work or rental housing affordable to extremely low through moderate income households in Eastern Madera County, developed in discussion with Self-Help Enterprises for Oakhurst. The funding source and subsequent awards were not identified in public records accessible this pass.
affordability_requirement: Affordable to extremely low, very low, low or moderate income households.
layering_notes: Madera County is a small non-entitlement county: the Community and Economic Development Department (planning, state CDBG and HOME applications) and Behavioral Health Services (BHSA, bridge housing) are the only County housing actors, the Housing Authority of the City of Madera (HACM) is the PHA for the county, and the Fresno Madera Continuum of Care (CA-514, led by Fresno County) handles HHAP and CoC funds. There is no County housing trust fund, NOFA, inclusionary ordinance or impact fee waiver program. The City of Madera is a separate CDBG and HOME entitlement with its own PLHA plan (Pass 3). maderacounty.com blocks automated access (403 on pages and documents), the PrimeGov and IQM2 portals returned no 2026 meetings, and Board agendas were read from PDFs mirrored on maderacountywater.com; other sources were HCD allocation tables, maderaha.org, zoneomics (County Code Title 18), CEQAnet and press coverage. This is the only discretionary County capital commitment to affordable housing found in the record; it signals willingness to fund a mountain-area project with a nonprofit developer. Source is the Fresnoland Board meeting report (October 4, 2021).

program_name: Behavioral Health Services Act Integrated Plan FY 2026-29: housing interventions and capital development
administering_agency: Monterey County Health Department, Behavioral Health Bureau
typical_award_size: Three-Year Integrated Plan and budget approved by the Board in June 2026 (Legistar file 26-552): Housing Interventions expenditures $9,025,327 (FY 2026-27), $9,296,089 (FY 2027-28) and $9,574,972 (FY 2028-29); capital development projects $1,130,582 rising to $1,199,435 a year (12.5% of the component); permanent rental subsidies $915,771 a year and interim rental subsidies $305,257 a year plus operating subsidies and a housing flex pool; 51.9% of housing funds dedicated to chronically homeless people; about 1,345 adults and 61 youth served a year.
affordability_requirement: BHSA eligible adults and youth with serious mental illness or substance use disorder; at least half of housing funds for chronically homeless people.
layering_notes: Monterey County's Housing and Community Development Department (HCD, Craig Spencer, Director; Darby Marshall, Housing Program Manager) runs the Inclusionary Housing Ordinance, the Monterey County Housing Trust Fund, PLHA, the Urban County CDBG and HOME programs and County land dispositions; the County Administrative Office Homelessness Strategies and Initiatives Division (CAO-HSI) runs HHAP and the SHARE Center; the Health Department Behavioral Health Bureau holds BHSA; the Coalition of Homeless Services Providers leads the CoC (CA-506, shared with San Benito); and the Housing Authority of the County of Monterey (HACM) and its Development Corporation supply vouchers and develop housing. Salinas, Monterey, Seaside and other entitlement cities run their own programs (Pass 3). countyofmonterey.gov blocks automated access (pages and documents), so records were built from the Legistar web API client 'monterey' and its Granicus attachments, hamonterey.org, chsp.org, zoneomics and HCD tables. Monterey is budgeting roughly $1.1 million a year of BHSA capital, enough for a small PSH gap or acquisition contribution, plus about $900,000 a year of permanent rental subsidies that can be project-based; pair with HHAP-6 operating money and HACM vouchers. Source is the June 2026 Integrated Plan approval item (Legistar file 26-552) with the budget attachment. Funding type set to grant because the Integrated Plan budget funds housing capital development ($1,130,582 in FY 2026-27, 12.5% of the Housing Interventions component) and rental, operating and bundled subsidies (rental subsidies $915,771 in FY 2026-27 rising to $971,542 in FY 2028-29).

program_name: Citrus Heights Affordable Housing Fee on commercial development (Resolution 2022-048) and City Housing Trust Fund
administering_agency: City of Citrus Heights Housing and Grants Division (fund); Building Division (fee collection)
typical_award_size: Fee source, not a subsidy program with published terms. Per the July 9, 2026 development impact fee sheet (Resolution 2022-048): office (including medical and assisted living) $1.95, hotel $2.35, commercial and retail $1.77, industrial (flex and R&D) $1.67 per square foot on new commercial development or added commercial square footage, applying to commercial projects both under and over 5,000 square feet; residential is exempt. Rates were raised in June 2022 to the regional average after no update since 1992. Revenue goes to the City Housing Trust Fund administered by the Housing and Grants Division; fund balance and any lending terms not published.
affordability_requirement: Unknown; linkage fee funds are for very low income housing per the original 1992 ordinance title (Nonresidential Construction Fees for Funding Very Low Income Housing).
layering_notes: Citrus Heights has no inclusionary ordinance and no residential affordable housing fee, and no city fee waiver program for affordable units was found; the fee sheet also lists multimodal ($1,591 per multifamily unit), park, Measure A transportation, drainage, sewer, school and fire fees that apply to apartments. The trust fund is small because the city is built out with little new commercial construction; the realistic city layer is the CDBG, HOME Consortium and PLHA record below plus SHRA bonds under a cooperation agreement.

program_name: West Sacramento Housing Development Corporation (City-affiliated nonprofit co-developer and property owner)
administering_agency: West Sacramento Housing Development Corporation (501(c)(3), EIN 94-3184534, 2950 Beacon Boulevard) working with the City Housing Division
typical_award_size: Partnership capacity rather than a funding program. The Housing Element names the West Sacramento Housing Development Corporation (WSHDC) alongside Yolo County Housing as the City's standing nonprofit partners for pursuing state and federal funds (Programs HE-PR-1.6 and 1.9). WSHDC co-developed West Gateway Place (77 units, 2017, $29.8 million) and West Gateway Place II / The Bridge at West Gateway (60 units, 2025) with Jamboree Housing on City-contributed land, and owns scattered rental properties managed by a third-party manager.
affordability_requirement: Projects to date serve 20% to 60% AMI families with permanent supportive units; terms set by the City and state funding.
layering_notes: For an outside developer WSHDC is the local partner that unlocks City land, Housing Trust Fund and HOME program income commitments and local-nonprofit scoring; Jamboree has been its repeat co-developer. Mercy Housing (Esperanza Crossing, CMFA bonds) and New Hope CDC (9% award for a West Sacramento project) have also worked in the city without WSHDC. Pair with Yolo County Housing PBVs and the welfare exemption (county records). WSHDC has no website; corporate facts are from nonprofit registries and the Jamboree fact sheet.

program_name: Jobs/Housing Impact Fee (commercial linkage fee), OMC Chapter 15.68, Fund 1871
administering_agency: City of Oakland Planning and Building Department (collection) and HCD (expenditure)
typical_award_size: Linkage fee on office and warehouse projects over 25,000 sq ft: $7.87 per sq ft for permits applied July 1, 2024 to June 30, 2025 per Table 4 ($8.05 for July 1, 2023 to June 30, 2024), inflation adjusted; paid 25% at permit, 50% at certificate of occupancy, 25% eighteen months later. The 2025 amendments extended the fee to additional nonresidential categories. FY 2024-25 JHIF fund (Fund 1871): start $13,964,433, end $12,546,460, fee revenue $0 in FY 2024-25, $12,060,074 committed to affordable developments, $486,386 being committed to pipeline projects. Past JHIF awards include $2,500,000 (2700 International, 75 units) and $3,472,130 (34th and San Pablo, 60 units).
affordability_requirement: Revenue restricted to acquisition, new construction, substantial rehabilitation and preservation of affordable housing, awarded through HCD NOFAs.
layering_notes: Oakland is one of only two priority cities in the county with a commercial linkage fee (Fremont also has one). Classified as loan because the fund balance is deployed as City development loans through HCD NOFAs (New Construction and ACAH); the fee itself is a cost to commercial developers, not to affordable housing sponsors. Revenue is modest relative to Measure U (FY 2024-25 JHIF fee revenue was $0) but is flexible local money with no bond restrictions, which HCD uses for early predevelopment commitments. Developers do not apply to this fund directly; it is part of the NOFA sources table.

program_name: Successor Housing Agency to the former Madera Redevelopment Agency (Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund)
administering_agency: City of Madera as Successor Housing Agency (Resolutions MRA-1498 and CC 12-09)
typical_award_size: Unknown. The City kept the former RDA's housing assets in January 2012, but the latest SB 341 annual reports posted are for FY 2014-15 and FY 2015-16. The FY 2015-16 report is a scanned PDF and its text could not be extracted. No current fund balance found.
affordability_requirement: Housing Asset Fund rules (HSC 34176.1): over each five-year period, at least 30% of development spending must serve extremely low income households and no more than 20% may serve households at 60-80% AMI.
layering_notes: Recorded so the asset fund is not overlooked. The 2026 Housing Element says losing redevelopment has limited the City's housing work, and it dropped one program for lack of funding, so little uncommitted cash likely remains. Any balance would add a small City layer next to HOME and PLHA. Confirm the fund balance and any housing successor-owned parcels before relying on it.

program_name: City of Ventura City-Owned and Publicly Owned Land for Housing and Affordable Housing Overlay (Housing Element Programs 23 and 24)
administering_agency: City of Ventura Community Development Department
typical_award_size: Land disposition or long-term lease of City sites (e.g., parking lots) via development agreements; no dollar figures.
affordability_requirement: Per disposition terms and the Surplus Land Act.
layering_notes: Ventura is near build-out, so public land is a main site source. The Housing Element also commits to continued funding of Housing Trust Fund Ventura County (Program 13; see County HTFVC record) and to exploring a business or parcel tax for housing. Needs confirmation because the city site blocked access.
